headline: Saudi Railways Awards Eastern Province Freight Extension to OHL Arabia and Hassan Allam
deck: Freight track in the Eastern Province is the least glamorous part of the rail programme and the part with the clearest industrial case.
excerpt: Saudi Arabia Railways has awarded a contract to extend its freight network in the Eastern Province to OHL Arabia and Hassan Allam Construction Saudi Arabia. The value and completion timeline have not been disclosed.
content:
Saudi Arabia Railways has awarded a contract to extend its freight railway network in the kingdom's Eastern Province to OHL Arabia and Hassan Allam Construction Saudi Arabia, according to RailFreight. Neither the contract value nor the completion timeline has been disclosed.

The Eastern Province is where the case for rail freight in Saudi Arabia is strongest and least dependent on forecast. It contains Jubail and Ras Al Khair, the ports at Dammam and King Fahd Industrial Port, the phosphate and bauxite chains that feed Ma'aden's processing complexes, and the petrochemical clusters that ship in bulk. These are commodities with high volume, low value density and predictable flows — the profile that rail carries more cheaply than road and that justifies fixed infrastructure.

That distinguishes freight extension work from the passenger schemes that attract more attention. A freight spur is judged on tonnage and on the cost per tonne-kilometre against trucking, not on journey time or ridership. Where an industrial customer already moves at scale between two fixed points, the calculation is straightforward, and the Eastern Province has more such pairs than anywhere else in the kingdom.

The contractor pairing is worth noting. OHL Arabia is the Saudi arm of the Spanish group, which has a long record in the kingdom's rail and civil infrastructure. Hassan Allam Construction Saudi Arabia is the Egyptian group's Saudi business, which has been widening its position in the market. Rail civils demand a specific competence — formation, drainage, structures built to alignment tolerances that ordinary highway work does not require — and the pool of contractors able to do it here is not large.

The award sits inside a wider rail programme that has been moving in stages. SAR is developing the Landbridge, a corridor of roughly 1,500 kilometres intended to connect Jeddah on the Red Sea with Dammam and Jubail on the Gulf, comprising around 950 kilometres of new railway between Jeddah and Riyadh and a further link of about 115 kilometres between Dammam and Jubail, alongside upgrades to existing track. Freight services on the corridor are planned to run at up to 160 kilometres per hour.

The Landbridge is being delivered in packages rather than as a single award, with construction tendered in stages as detailed engineering progresses and completion targeted for 2034. An Eastern Province freight extension awarded now is consistent with that sequencing: the eastern end of the corridor is where existing network and existing demand already are, so work there can proceed while the longer western sections are still being engineered.

For the industrial customers along the route, the significance is in modal capacity rather than in any single line. Saudi ports have been adding container services and the kingdom has set a target of 40 million TEU of annual throughput by 2030, a volume that cannot be moved inland by road alone. Freight rail is the constraint that has to be relieved for port expansion to convert into industrial throughput, and extensions in the Eastern Province are where that relief begins.

SAR has not said when work will start on site.
author: Jakson Gudawela
